chapter.name: Differential Equations
chapter.blurb: An equation involving derivatives of the dependent variable with respect to an independent variable is called a differential equation. The chapter studies the order and degree of a differential equation, its general and particular solutions, and three methods of solving first order, first degree differential equations: variables separable, homogeneous equations and linear equations, with applications to curves, compound interest and growth.

scope_in.item: Recognise a differential equation as an equation involving derivatives of the dependent variable, and an ordinary differential equation as one with derivatives with respect to a single independent variable; use the notations y', y'', y''' and dy/dx, d^2y/dx^2
Find the order of a differential equation as the order of its highest order derivative
Decide whether the degree is defined (polynomial equation in the derivatives) and, if so, find it as the highest power of the highest order derivative; know order and degree are positive integers
Verify that a given explicit or implicit function is a solution of a differential equation by substituting it and its derivatives
Distinguish the general solution (as many arbitrary constants as the order) from a particular solution (free from arbitrary constants); count arbitrary constants
Solve first order, first degree equations dy/dx = g(x) h(y) by separating the variables, find particular solutions and curves through a given point

Apply the variable separable method to slope-of-tangent curve problems, continuous compound interest, bacterial growth proportional to the number present and a balloon inflating at a constant volume rate
Test whether F(x, y) is a homogeneous function of degree n using F(lambda x, lambda y) = lambda^n F(x, y), and whether dy/dx = F(x, y) or dx/dy = G(x, y) is a homogeneous differential equation
Solve homogeneous differential equations by y = vx (or x = vy for dx/dy = h(x/y)), including particular solutions and families of curves defined by a slope

Recognise first order linear equations dy/dx + Py = Q and dx/dy + P1 x = Q1, find the integrating factor e^(integral of P dx) or e^(integral of P1 dy), and write general and particular solutions, including curves from a slope condition

scope_out.item: Formation of a differential equation whose general solution is given (eliminating arbitrary constants from a family of curves)
scope_out.reason: Not present in this rationalised Reprint 2026-27 edition: section 9.3 (General and Particular Solutions, pp. 304-306) is followed directly by 9.4 Methods of Solving (p. 306). The introduction on p. 300 still mentions 'formation of differential equations', but no section, example or exercise teaches it
Named on p. 301 only to say 'at this stage we shall confine ourselves to the study of ordinary differential equations only'

scope_out.item: Methods of solving second or higher order differential equations
scope_out.reason: Second order equations appear only for order/degree and for verifying a given solution (pp. 302-306, 329-330, 334); every solving method in 9.4 is for first order, first degree equations (p. 306)

scope_out.item: Degree of an equation containing radicals of derivatives (clearing fractional powers before reading the degree)
scope_out.reason: The book defines degree only for equations that are already polynomial in the derivatives (p. 302) and never discusses rationalising; questions avoid such equations

scope_out.item: Equations reducible to homogeneous form by shifting the origin, e.g. (4x + 6y + 5) dy = (3y + 2x + 4) dx
scope_out.reason: Appears only as a non-homogeneous option in Exercise 9.4 Q17 (p. 322); the book never solves such equations

scope_out.item: Exact equations, Bernoulli equations, Clairaut's equation and integrating factors other than e^(integral of P dx)
scope_out.reason: The only methods in 9.4 are variables separable, homogeneous and linear (p. 306); the substitution x - y = t appears once as a hint in Miscellaneous Exercise Q9 (p. 335) and is not developed as a method

scope_out.item: Newton's law of cooling, radioactive decay half-life, orthogonal trajectories and mixing problems
scope_out.reason: The applications in this edition are limited to slope-of-tangent curves, continuous compound interest, bacterial growth and an inflating balloon (pp. 309-313, 327-329)

concepts.name: Differential equations and their order
concepts.description: Recognising a differential equation as an equation involving derivatives of the dependent variable, ordinary differential equations, and finding the order as the order of the highest order derivative present.
concepts.idea: A differential equation links an unknown function with its derivatives; its order says how many times, at most, the dependent variable has been differentiated in it.
concepts.rule: Order = order of the highest order derivative of the dependent variable present in the equation. It is always a positive integer and does not depend on the powers to which the derivatives are raised.
concepts.example: d^3y/dx^3 + x^2 (d^2y/dx^2)^3 = 0 has order 3, because d^3y/dx^3 is the highest order derivative present.

concepts.name: Degree of a differential equation
concepts.description: Deciding whether the degree of a differential equation is defined (the equation must be a polynomial equation in its derivatives) and, when it is, finding it as the highest power of the highest order derivative.
concepts.idea: Degree only makes sense when the derivatives appear as in a polynomial; then it records the power of the highest order derivative.
concepts.rule: If the equation is a polynomial equation in y', y'', y''', ..., its degree is the highest positive integral power of the highest order derivative. If a derivative sits inside sin, cos, e^( ) and the like, the degree is not defined. Order and degree (if defined) are always positive integers.
concepts.example: (dy/dx)^2 + dy/dx - sin^2 y = 0 has degree 2 (it is a polynomial in y', though not in y), while dy/dx + sin(dy/dx) = 0 has no degree.

concepts.name: General and particular solutions
concepts.description: Verifying that a given function (explicit or implicit) is a solution of a differential equation by substitution, and telling a general solution (with arbitrary constants) from a particular solution (constants given values).
concepts.idea: A solution of a differential equation is a function, not a number: substitute it and its derivatives and the two sides must agree.
concepts.rule: The general solution contains as many arbitrary constants as the order of the equation; a particular solution is obtained by giving particular values to these constants and is free from arbitrary constants.
concepts.example: y = a sin(x + b) is the general solution of d^2y/dx^2 + y = 0 (two constants, order 2); y = 2 sin(x + pi/4) is a particular solution.

questions.q: Verify that y = a cos x + b sin x, where a and b are real constants, is a solution of d^2y/dx^2 + y = 0.

s: Differentiates twice to get d^2y/dx^2 = -a cos x - b sin x

questions.q: Verify that y = x sin 3x is a solution of the differential equation d^2y/dx^2 + 9y - 6 cos 3x = 0.
questions.a: dy/dx = sin 3x + 3x cos 3x. d^2y/dx^2 = 3 cos 3x + 3 cos 3x - 9x sin 3x = 6 cos 3x - 9x sin 3x. Then d^2y/dx^2 + 9y - 6 cos 3x = 6 cos 3x - 9x sin 3x + 9x sin 3x - 6 cos 3x = 0 = R.H.S.
s: Finds dy/dx = sin 3x + 3x cos 3x using the product rule

questions.q: Check which of y = e^x, y = e^(-x) and y = e^(2x) satisfy y'' - y = 0. Using the ones that do, write a solution containing two arbitrary constants and say what kind of solution it is.
questions.a: For y = e^x: y'' - y = e^x - e^x = 0, a solution. For y = e^(-x): y'' = e^(-x), so y'' - y = 0, a solution. For y = e^(2x): y'' - y = 4e^(2x) - e^(2x) = 3e^(2x), not 0, so it is not a solution. Then y = A e^x + B e^(-x) gives y'' = A e^x + B e^(-x) = y, so it is a solution; it has two arbitrary constants, equal to the order 2, so it is the general solution.
s: Shows e^x and e^(-x) satisfy the equation
Shows e^(2x) does not
Writes y = A e^x + B e^(-x), verifies it and calls it the general solution (2 constants = order 2)

questions.q: A student claims that y = cos x + C cannot satisfy y' + sin x = 0 for every value of C, because the constant C would be left over. Is the student right? Justify.
questions.a: No. The derivative of the constant C is 0, so y' = -sin x for every C, and y' + sin x = 0. So y = cos x + C satisfies the equation for every C; it is the general solution of this first order equation.
s: Notes the derivative of C is 0 so y' = -sin x
Concludes it satisfies the equation for every C, so the student is wrong

questions.q: The general solution of d^2y/dx^2 + y = 0 is y = a cos x + b sin x. Construct the particular solution with y = 0 when x = 0 and y = 3 when x = pi/2, and verify it.
questions.a: At x = 0: y = a = 0. At x = pi/2: y = b = 3. So y = 3 sin x. Check: y'' = -3 sin x, so y'' + y = 0, and y(0) = 0, y(pi/2) = 3.
s: Uses y(0) = 0 to get a = 0
Uses y(pi/2) = 3 to get b = 3, so y = 3 sin x
Verifies y = 3 sin x satisfies the equation and both conditions

concepts.name: Variables separable method
concepts.description: Solving dy/dx = g(x) h(y) by separating the variables and integrating both sides, finding particular solutions and curves through a point, and applying it to continuous growth (bank interest, bacteria) and rate problems.
concepts.idea: If the right side splits into a function of x times a function of y, move all the y terms to dy and all the x terms to dx, then integrate each side.
concepts.rule: dy/dx = g(x) h(y), h(y) not 0, gives integral of dy/h(y) = integral of g(x) dx, i.e. H(y) = G(x) + C. Use a given point or condition to fix C for a particular solution.
concepts.example: dy/dx = -4xy^2 gives dy/y^2 = -4x dx, so -1/y = -2x^2 + C; with y = 1 at x = 0, C = -1 and y = 1/(2x^2 + 1).

questions.q: In a culture the bacteria count is 1,00,000. It increases by 10% in 2 hours. If the rate of growth is proportional to the number present, in how many hours will the count reach 2,00,000?
questions.a: Let y be the count at time t hours. dy/dt = ky, so dy/y = k dt and y = C e^(kt). At t = 0, y = 100000, so C = 100000. At t = 2, y = 110000: e^(2k) = 1.1, so k = (1/2) log 1.1. For y = 200000: e^(kt) = 2, so t = (log 2)/k = 2 log 2/log 1.1 hours (about 14.5 hours).
s: Sets up dy/dt = ky and solves to y = C e^(kt) with C = 100000
Uses the 10% rise in 2 hours to get k = (1/2) log 1.1
Solves e^(kt) = 2 to get t = 2 log 2/log 1.1 hours

concepts.name: Homogeneous functions and homogeneous differential equations
concepts.description: Testing whether F(x, y) is a homogeneous function of degree n by replacing x, y with lambda x, lambda y, and deciding whether dy/dx = F(x, y) (or dx/dy = G(x, y)) is a homogeneous differential equation, i.e. F is homogeneous of degree zero.
concepts.idea: A homogeneous function scales by a fixed power of lambda when both variables are scaled by lambda; a homogeneous differential equation has a right side of degree zero, so it depends only on y/x.
concepts.rule: F(x, y) is homogeneous of degree n if F(lambda x, lambda y) = lambda^n F(x, y), equivalently F = x^n g(y/x) or y^n h(x/y). dy/dx = F(x, y) is homogeneous if F is homogeneous of degree zero.
concepts.example: y^2 + 2xy is homogeneous of degree 2, 2x - 3y of degree 1, cos(y/x) of degree 0, while sin x + cos y is not homogeneous.

concepts.name: Solving homogeneous differential equations
concepts.description: Solving dy/dx = g(y/x) by the substitution y = vx (and dx/dy = h(x/y) by x = vy), separating v and x, integrating, and replacing v by y/x; finding particular solutions and families of curves.
concepts.idea: In a homogeneous equation only the ratio y/x matters, so treating that ratio v as the new unknown turns the equation into a separable one.
concepts.rule: Put y = vx, so dy/dx = v + x dv/dx. Then x dv/dx = g(v) - v, so dv/(g(v) - v) = dx/x; integrate and replace v by y/x. For dx/dy = h(x/y) put x = vy, dx/dy = v + y dv/dy.

concepts.name: Linear differential equations and the integrating factor
concepts.description: Recognising first order linear differential equations dy/dx + Py = Q (P, Q functions of x) or dx/dy + P1 x = Q1 (P1, Q1 functions of y), finding the integrating factor, and writing general and particular solutions, including curves defined by a slope condition.
concepts.idea: Multiplying a linear equation by the right factor turns its left side into the derivative of y times that factor, so one integration solves it.
concepts.rule: For dy/dx + Py = Q: I.F. = e^(integral of P dx), and y (I.F.) = integral of Q (I.F.) dx + C. For dx/dy + P1 x = Q1: I.F. = e^(integral of P1 dy), and x (I.F.) = integral of Q1 (I.F.) dy + C. Put the equation in standard form (coefficient of dy/dx equal to 1) before reading off P.
concepts.example: x dy/dx + 2y = x^2: divide by x to get P = 2/x, I.F. = e^(2 log x) = x^2, so y x^2 = x^4/4 + C.
